items.title: Matthew Day, Executive Director, WR Community Energy
notes:
The delegate provided a presentation on energy resiliency in Waterloo Region, and the work his organization is doing to leverage assets to support energy programs. He elaborated on existing energy programs and future proposals in the works to assist with efficient energy use.

In reply to questions from the Committee, the delegate spoke to perceptible resistance to certain energy programs, and although Canada is an energy powerhouse, much of the energy does not make its way to Kitchener-Waterloo area. He further elaborated on measures to enhance the inherent energy quality in the area. 

In response to a question from the Committee, the delegate spoke to design patterns in house construction currently, in terms of energy efficiency. He elaborated that lots of houses are being built to sell, not to live in, and that energy costs are not necessarily prioritized. The delegate indicated that his organization's goal is for future houses to be built with energy efficiency in mind.

Replying to a question from the Committee, the delegate spoke to thermal energy strategies, and explained that this is a more collaborative program, with his organization contributing research and ideas.

In reply to a question from the Committee, the delegate indicated Artificial Intelligence is being investigated for energy efficiency, with developers already approaching his organization with these types of things in place.

items.title: PDL-AIR-25-001, Economic Impact Study of the Region of Waterloo International Airport (YKF)
notes:
Rod Regier, Commissioner, Planning, Development, and Legislative Services, provided an introduction to the report and introduced the consultant, InterVISTAS, who conducted the study. Doris Mak and Celina Estrella, consultants with InterVISTAS, provided a presentation which elaborated on the results of the study, indicating the overall economic benefit created from the Region of Waterloo international airport.

In reply to a question from the Committee, R. Regier indicated that the airport has started the analysis with the Rick Hansen Foundation in 2024  for accessibility, and that the airport is receiving its certification the next day, April 9th, 2025.

In response to a question from the Committee, R. Regier confirmed that the taxes are collected by the Township and go through to the Region, showing that 98% of the taxes collected go to other levels of government. R. Regier added that the airport has been successful at attracting investment from the federal government, and Transport Canada has contributed to airport parking centers, as well as two firetrucks. 

R. Regier explained that the sustainability program forms a serious part of the work with the airport, and that the carbon footprint is being monitored along with its budget. An updated Master Plan is coming for the airport which has significant sustainability initiatives, which is expected to come back in the June cycle.

Replying to a question from the Committee, R. Regier explained that the parking lot is going to be opened in May, and that the large overflow lot has space for about 800 cars, and it gets significant use during the peak seasons. There is less parking demands during the off-peak seasons which is managed at the main terminal. He reiterated that the parking rates were increased last year, and that parking is a significant source of revenue.

items.title: TSD-TRS-25-005, GRT Business Plan
notes:
D. Spooner provided an introduction to the report, elaborating on the goals and engagement associated with this major process. He recognized the work done by the entire GRT team, and celebrated the recipients of national awards on the team. Kevan Marshall, Manager, Transit Development, provided a presentation on the different sections of the GRT business plan, and the various priorities outlined within the plan. He elaborated on the community engagement conducted as well as the new and existing service plans.

In reply to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner spoke to the efficacy of the Affordable Transit Program, utilizing income tested means to distribute the discounts to those who need it most. In terms of the specialized transit plan, Neil Malcolm, Acting Director, Transit Services, clarified that 24/7 accessible taxi services are being explored. Staff were given direction to connect with Regional By-law staff about accessible service options at the Region.

Responding to questions from the Committee, D. Spooner clarified that statistics about automobile and transit use can be included in the report. He also elaborated on the financial impact of the plan, and framed the discussion based on service expansion. He indicated this is a scalable plan based on the will of Council. He further explained the area-rating system, with the Township taking the cost of transit going within their boundaries. He stressed that staff are focused on a respectful and benefit-driven approach to transit in the Townships.

In reply to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner answered that Cambridge residents are paying for the LRT due to the relation to the broader central transit corridor, and that the rapid transit report initial business case is coming in November. In terms of Cambridge to Guelph rail service, documents will be submitted to the provincial minister within a week from the meeting. Furthermore, D. Spooner explained that electrification will be included for the proposed Cambridge system.

Responding to the Committee, K. Marshall identified opportunities to collaborate with community partners to encourage the ministry to prioritize public transit in funding arrangements. Furthermore, N. Malcolm spoke to technical differences between articulated versus other types of buses, and the procurement for various types based on demand and capability. Staff were given direction to provide information on transit for the Vista Hills neighbourhood with the final proposed version of the GRT Business Plan.

In reply to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner spoke to the senior or veteran option for less expensive passes, in which there are currently 2 programs for seniors. Furthermore, D. Spooner indicated that financial impacts of the federal election are being considered, but that major changes are not currently anticipated. A request was made that Regional staff make an effort to present to area municipality Councils' regarding this report. D. Spooner spoke to timing challenges for visiting all municipalities, but indicated the effort could be made and added that more information is expected to come in the fall of 2025 regarding implementation of the plan.

In response to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner spoke to the collaboration with the Kiwanis service to the GRT system, and that the end goal is to ensure one service point while maintaining independence.

Staff were asked about providing more information regarding a cost-benefit analysis for the impacts of the implementation of this plan.

items.title: Notice of Motion - Councillor S. Shantz
notes:
S. Shantz introduced her motion and spoke to the residents' concern. She expressed that although traffic calming is supported, there may be solutions better suited for Lobsinger Line. J. Nowak expanded on the needs for his community related to speed cameras.

In response to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner underlined the philosophy behind the 40 km/h speed limit, with safety concerns increasing significantly at 60 km/h. He indicated that areas such as the one outlined in the motion score well for municipal speed camera use due to the reduction of speed. D. Spooner elaborated that with the passing of the motion, two locations would need to be adjusted, and that the cameras in those areas are not issuing tickets. He explained that staff may need more guidance on specific action for this motion since other actions are being taken to implement the Automated Speed Enforcement program. D. Spooner clarified that he would interpret the third clause to mean "rural roads," for clarity.

Replying to a question from the Committee, D. Spooner indicated that there have been two collisions in each area identified in the motion, with 1 fatal collision. He indicated there have been multiple drivers found speeding above 130 km/h since the camera's were implemented. He also spoke to a fatality of a road crew member in Hamilton, and a near miss on Northfield Drive. Consequently, he would like the opportunity to report back on this program to speak to the implications of changing the speed to 60 km/h. Additionally, he pointed to road design as an alternative to slow speeds.

motions.item_title: Notice of Motion - Councillor S. Shantz
motions.text: Whereas the prevailing narrative is that road speeds should reflect what a driver would naturally expect to drive; and Whereas the two rural roads that we have reduced the school zone speed from 80 to 60 to 40 have created dangerous driving situations endangering both drivers and other road users; and Whereas the lower speed limits at rural schools are only needed during school hours; and Whereas rural roads have different traffic patterns and expectations than urban roads; That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo: Prepare the requisite amending by-law(s) to lower speed limits in school zones from 80 km/h to 60 km/h (instead of the current 40 km/h) on Lobsinger Line near King Alfred Academy and Northfield Drive near Balsam Grove Parochial School.
motions.text_html:
Whereas the prevailing narrative is that road speeds should reflect what a driver would naturally expect to drive; and
Whereas the two rural roads that we have reduced the school zone speed from 80 to 60 to 40 have created dangerous driving situations endangering  both drivers and other road users; and
Whereas the lower speed limits at rural schools are only needed during school hours; and
Whereas rural roads have different traffic patterns and expectations than urban roads;

That the Regional Municipality of Waterloo:

  1. Prepare the requisite amending by-law(s) to lower speed limits in school zones from 80 km/h to 60 km/h (instead of the current 40 km/h) on Lobsinger Line near King Alfred Academy and Northfield Drive near Balsam Grove Parochial School.
